extracted.intended_audience: researchers and students in experimental humor psychology / cognitive social psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Laboratory experiments testing how priming, serial presentation (switch vs stay), and personality (Sensation Seeking, Conservatism) affect ratings of cartoon 'funniness' and 'aversiveness' for two humor structures (INC-RES and NON).

rubrics_metrics.name: Funniness rating scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Funniness was rated as 0 = not at all funny to 6 = very funny; each cartoon presented on a separate page with spaces for reporting funniness scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants were instructed that funniness is independent from aversiveness; ratings taken for each cartoon separately and analyzed (e.g., sumscores, trial-by-trial, difference scores).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aversiveness rating scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Aversiveness was rated as 0 = not at all aversive to 6 = very aversive; defined to participants as a general negative response indicating that a cartoon is distasteful for some reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimenter explicitly explained the meaning of 'aversive' (some participants did not know the term); emphasized that a cartoon can vary independently on funniness and aversiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate measurement of funniness and aversiveness (orthogonality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Funniness and aversiveness were treated as two independent measures of humor appreciation (Ruch, 1992 suggests orthogonality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirically these measures may correlate for some structures (e.g., NON) and not for others (e.g., INC-RES); investigators should both instruct participants about independence and examine correlations before assuming orthogonality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulus selection from 3WD humor scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartoons were selected from the 3WD (forms A and B) humor scale (Ruch, 1983) as the best examples of INC-RES and NON based on correlational analyses from Experiment 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select stimuli whose individual correlations for funniness and aversiveness align with theoretical predictions; appendices list the cartoons used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Randomization and Latin square control for order effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Each tested group was subdivided into four small groups with Latin square randomized orders of cartoon presentations so that across groups no cartoon was in the same position for more than one grouping and no cartoon was followed by the same cartoon in more than one grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content and cartoon randomization is 'critical for inferences concerning the context effects of structural presentation'; use Latin squares to control serial-position and adjacency confounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priming manipulation and group definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two control groups (single structure presentation) and two experimental groups (primed with one structure and switched to the second structure on the final trial): NON only control, INC-RES only control, NON→INC-RES experimental, INC-RES→NON experimental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design priming so that primed structure is presented repeatedly (first three trials) with the 'switch' on the fourth trial to test state/priming effects; ensure group sizes and sex composition are reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of MANOVA for funniness and aversiveness analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Funniness and aversiveness ratings were analyzed by separate 2 (prime structure) × 2 (switch condition) × 4 (trials) MANOVAs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report between-groups and within-subjects main effects and interactions; note when MANOVA is not a direct test of a specific hypothesis (use planned comparisons where necessary); report Pillai's approximate F when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planned comparison difference-score ANOVA
rubrics_metrics.description: A planned-comparison ANOVA used a difference score (rating of fourth cartoon minus mean of first three cartoon ratings) to test effects of priming with one structure on the first three trials and switching on the fourth trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use difference-score contrasts when MANOVA does not directly test the hypothesized prime-by-switch effect; interpret significant interactions in terms of priming/switch effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference score operationalization and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Difference score (DSCR): positive DSCR indicates increased funniness or aversiveness for the final cartoon; negative DSCR indicates decreased funniness or aversiveness for the final cartoon; zero shows no preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use DSCR as an overall dependent measure of preference due to priming effects and correlate with personality variables; report direction and magnitude (and significance) of DSCR associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sumscores for first-three cartoons as preference measures
rubrics_metrics.description: A sum of the first three cartoons (all subjects rated either all INC-RES or all NON on the first three cartoons) was used as a dependent measure of preference for the individual structures (NON sumscore and INC-RES sumscore).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sumscores to assess trait-like preferences and to correlate or regress on personality predictors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlational analyses with personality predictors
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple correlations between Sensation Seeking and Conservatism scales and difference scores and sumscores were calculated to assess relationships between personality and appreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present correlation matrices (tables) separately for NON and INC-RES; interpret correlations in the context of theoretical predictions (e.g., tolerance for ambiguity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple regression prediction from personality scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple regression analyses were used to predict preference (sumscores) from Sensation Seeking (Zuckerman, 1979) and Conservatism (Wilson, 1973); report R squared, unstandardized b, t, p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report which structure's funniness or aversiveness is predicted (e.g., regressions significant for NON funniness only in this study) and the relative contribution of each predictor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and operationalization of personality measures (tolerance for ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensation Seeking (Zuckerman, 1979) and Conservatism (Wilson, 1973) are used as measures of personality-based tolerance for ambiguity; high Sensation Seeking / low Conservatism = tolerant, low Sensation Seeking / high Conservatism = intolerant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These scales can be used as continuous predictors or to create extreme groups for between-subjects comparisons (Experiment 2 uses extreme scoring).

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant procedures: testing, consent, debriefing
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects tested as a large group in an auditorium; rating scales explained; asked to read and sign consent form (anonymous and no deception) if they wished to participate; upon completion thanked, debriefed, and solicited for questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure participants understand scale definitions and consent is voluntary and anonymous; provide debriefing and opportunity for questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit explanation of terminology to participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Because some Ss indicated they did not know what 'aversive' meant, the experimenter indicated that aversiveness is a general negative response indicating a cartoon is distasteful for some reason; stressed that cartoons could differ on the two scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When uncommon terms are used as dependent measures, provide clear operational definitions and examples to participants to avoid measurement error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis specification (cognitive 'state', personality 'trait', complementary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses are explicitly stated: cognitive 'state' hypotheses (priming increases salience; switch cartoons should be rated differently; aversiveness influenced by priming), personality hypothesis (Sensation Seekers vs Conservatives differ in preferences), and complementary hypothesis (interaction of context, structure, personality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State both general and directional predictions to guide planned comparisons and regression analyses; link predictions to theory (salience hypothesis, dual process theory, Forabosco's sequence rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of content effects and acknowledgment of error variance
rubrics_metrics.description: Because cartoons varied in content, randomization of cartoon content was used to control for content effects; randomization yielded a large amount of error variance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control for content by randomizing and counterbalancing stimulus order; be prepared for increased error variance and report its likely influence on effect sizes and power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longer series and switch-position manipulations to test habituation/sensitization
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment 2 uses a longer series of cartoons and varies position of the 'switch' cartoon to test dual-process predictions (sensitization then habituation), with habituation predicted between the third and fifth cartoon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To test habituation, extend series beyond four trials and include conditions that omit or vary switch position; compare trajectories across trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming extreme personality groups for clearer trait tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Personality was experimentally defined by categorizing scores on the personality measures and using extreme scores to form personality groups in Experiment 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extreme-group methodology to increase power to detect personality × structure interactions, recognizing trade-offs in generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of contrast effects and structure salience
rubrics_metrics.description: A contrast effect for appreciation may explain ANOVA interactions: less congruous structure (NON) primes appreciation for more congruous structure (INC-RES), while INC-RES interferes with appreciation for NON; structure salience influences appreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting interactions, consider contrast/salience explanations in addition to simple priming; analyze pattern of means (e.g., fourth-trial differences) to infer contrast vs. habituation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical reporting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Report statistics as F(df) = value, p < threshold; indicate use of Pillai's approximate F for MANOVAs; report significance levels (e.g., * p < .05, ** p < .01, ** p < .001) and effect-size indicators (R squared).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow clear statistical reporting standards and include exact p-values, degrees of freedom, and effect-size measures where possible.
